You are urban_comet97, one of 10 agents working together on the same task on a shared platform. All
10 agents form one group, and you work with brisk_harbor75, early_island22, gentle_otter27, jolly_ember22, pale_kettle84, pale_lantern48, rapid_thistle87, sandy_walnut42, zesty_lantern63. Each agent works in its own sandbox, on its
own git repository. Your group shares one `main` branch, which every member can push to, and one channel
(`group`). Work together with your teammates to make your group's `main` as good as possible. Use `group` to
coordinate and share helpful findings.

## Setting
Your task is to recreate a program from scratch based only on its observable behavior and bundled documentation.
You are given a reference executable and its documentation.
Treat the reference executable as a specification you can query through its normal user interface.

Your submission must be an independent implementation.
Using the original source code, wrapping the reference executable, or installing an existing implementation does not satisfy the task and will receive no credit.
It will be detected by an automated judge, marked as a disqualification, and scored as a failure.

<RULES>
## What is NOT allowed

### 1. Using an existing implementation

The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its
bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.
- Fetching source tarballs from project websites (e.g., `curl https://lua.org/ftp/lua-5.5.0.tar.gz`)
- Using a package manager to download the project as a dependency and then reading its cached source (e.g., navigating into `~/.cargo/registry/src/` or `$(go env GOPATH)/pkg/mod/`)
- Searching the web for the project's source code or implementation details

### 2. Wrapping or reusing the reference executable

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The reference `/opt/reference/executable` is for
observation only — your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the reference executable (e.g., `exec zstd "$@"`)
- Installing the tool from a package manager and shimming to it (e.g., `apt-get install nnn && cp $(which nnn) ./executable`)
- Writing a `compile.sh` that only runs `chmod +x ./executable` or copies the reference executable (`cp ./executable ./executable`)
- Building a binary whose main function shells out to an external tool (e.g., `Command::new("miniserve").args(args).exec()`)
- Re-linking prebuilt `.o` object files found in the workspace without writing new source code

### 3. How the reference executable may be observed

All information about the reference `/opt/reference/executable` must be obtained by interacting with it
through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).
- You MUST NOT decompile `/opt/reference/executable` or use disassemblers (objdump, Ghidra, etc.) on it
- You MUST NOT use strace, ltrace, or similar tracing/instrumentation tools on `/opt/reference/executable`

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the reference `/opt/reference/executable`. You are free to use any
analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

## What IS allowed

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace
</RULES>

## Your repository and your group's main
- In your sandbox, `/workspace` is your own git repository, and the reference executable is in `/opt/reference`. No one else can see it.
- Your group's shared `main` is the remote `team`. Fetch it with `git fetch team` (you get `team/main`),
  and push to it with `git push team HEAD:main`. **Your local files do not update automatically when a
  teammate pushes.**
- A push must be a fast-forward: if `main` has moved since you last fetched, the push is rejected. Fetch,
  merge `team/main` into your work, and push again.
- When you push, the platform posts in `group` on your behalf, with your commit message, a summary of the
  changed files, and a pointer to the new `main`. Write commit messages that say what changed.
- Your git name and email are preconfigured as your agent name. Do not change them.
- Commit with `git commit -m "<message>"`: there is no editor in the sandbox, so a commit without `-m`
  fails with an empty message.
- Run the reference executable and your experiments outside `/workspace` (for example in `/tmp`), so that they do not change your
  repository.

## Scoring rule
Your payoff is your group's final score: the fraction of hidden tests passed by the code on `main` at
the end. Every agent receives the same payoff.
- **Only the code on your group's `main` at the end is graded.** Code in your own repository, or shared
  through pointers, does not count until it is pushed to `main`. If no one pushes, the initial commit is
  graded.
- Everyone keeps working until time runs out.

## Platform
The platform is the shared place where agents announce what they are exploring, building, or have found,
and ask each other questions. Typical posts include a direction you are exploring, a component you are
building, a finding (how the original program behaves in some case, a useful test command, a tricky edge case), a proposal for how to organize the work, or a question.
- `post` publishes a message to `group`, with a title: a one-line summary of the message, up
  to 120 characters. Every post gets a number. Mention someone with @name.
- To share code, commit it, then list it in the post's `attach`. The platform adds a pointer
  (`[[<sha>:<path>#La-b]]`) to the post for each item. `attach` can name:
  - `path#La-b`: a file in your `HEAD`, optionally with a line range;
  - `<sha>:path#La-b`: a file in another commit;
  - a commit's sha, or `HEAD`: a whole commit;
  - `file:<path>#La-b`: the current content of a single file, even if it is not committed. Readers see
    only that file.
  Pointing at a commit makes all files in that commit readable. Uncommitted changes are not shared.
- `read_feed` lists the new posts in `group`, and any unopened posts that mention you, one line each
  (number, author, channel, title). `read_feed` with a post's number shows its full text, with its
  pointers expanded into the code and a diff against your own version.
- You can fetch any code shared with you into your repository with `git fetch origin` (as
  `origin/shared/<author>/<sha>`), and then merge or cherry-pick what you want.

After each action, a platform notice lists the new posts on the channels you can read, one line each (number,
author, channel, title, and a marker when the post carries code). A post that mentions you appears in
every notice until you open it with `read_feed` and its number.

## Working together
- Start by **getting an overview of what the reference program supports**, enough to understand how the
  program should behave in its main cases, and share it in `group` as a list (if a teammate has
  already posted one, add to theirs), so the group can keep extending the plan and everyone stays up
  to date on which areas are covered. Then **agree with your teammates on how to work together**:
  split the work, or have several members build the same part and compare, keeping the best of each.
  If parts depend on each other, agree on the interfaces first, and while you wait for a part you
  need, write tests for it with expected output from the reference program.
- If a teammate has already posted a plan, **follow it and propose changes to it** instead of posting
  a competing one.
- Work in a cycle: (1) pick an area and say so in `group`; (2) build it on top of the latest `main`;
  (3) compare its output with the reference program on the same inputs; (4) commit, `git fetch team`, merge
  `team/main`, and `git push team HEAD:main`; (5) post what you finished, with a pointer, then go back
  to (1). Report a part as done only once it is on `main`: a part that is not on `main` does not count.
- Passing your own tests does not mean the task is done: always assume the hidden tests cover more
  than your tests do. **When your tests all pass, test more areas.** Add cases for features and
  options your tests do not cover yet, including the parts your teammates are handling. A new area
  usually matters more than more cases in an area that already works.
- **Never stop calling tool before time is up. When you are not sure what to do next, review the
  whole program on `main` again** as a reviewer looking for bugs: features of the reference program that
  are missing or only partly handled, edge cases (empty input, `null`, deep nesting, large numbers,
  unusual option combinations), and error paths. Do not review only your own part: test the whole
  program, including your teammates' parts, with inputs you have not tried yet. Test each suspicion
  against the reference program, and fix what differs.
- **If one approach keeps failing, change the approach instead of retrying it.** Post in `group` what
  you tried, so teammates do not repeat it and can suggest other ideas. If you are still stuck, put a
  version that handles the common cases on `main` for now, and come back to it later.
- Do not leave hard parts as known gaps. Come back to them, discuss them with your teammates, and solve as
  many of them as possible: **keep improving `main` until time runs out.**

Write it in **Python 3.10**.

- Write your implementation in your own workspace `/workspace`, starting from `/workspace/main.py`.
  You may add more Python modules next to it. **Standard library only.**
- `/workspace/compile.sh` is already provided: at evaluation time it turns `main.py` into the program under

- Your implementation is scored on hidden tests that compare its behavior against the original.

**Recommended workflow:** read the documentation, run the original program to learn its behavior, then write
the code. Start writing `main.py` early and grow it incrementally: an incomplete implementation that
handles the common cases scores far better than none. After each change, run your code against the
original to check it. If an approach keeps failing, step back and consider other causes before trying
again.

I’ll inspect the bundled docs and the existing team feed first to see what the program supports and whether work has already been divided up. Then I’ll claim an uncovered area, probe the reference, and implement it on top of the latest shared code.

# Dasel Dasel (short for **Data-Select**) is a command-line tool and library for querying, modifying, and transforming data structures such as JSON, YAML, TOML, XML, CSV, and KDL. It provides a consistent, powerful syntax to traverse and update data — making it useful for developers, DevOps, and data wrangling tasks. --- ## Features * **Multi-format support**: JSON, YAML, TOML, XML, CSV, HCL, INI, KDL. * **Unified query syntax**: Access data in any format with the same selectors. * **Query & search**: Extract values, lists, or structures with intuitive syntax. * **Modify in place**: Update, insert, or delete values directly in structured files. * **Convert between formats**: Seamlessly transform data from JSON → YAML, TOML → JSON, etc. * **Script-friendly**: Simple CLI integration for shell scripts and pipelines. * **Library support**: Import and use in Go projects. --- ## Installation ### Homebrew (macOS/Linux) ```sh brew install dasel ``` ### Go Install ```sh go install github.com/tomwright/dasel/v3/cmd/dasel@master ``` ### Prebuilt Binaries Prebuilt binaries are available on the [Releases](https://github.com/TomWright/dasel/releases) page for Linux, macOS, and Windows. ### None of the above? See the [installation docs](https://daseldocs.tomwright.me/getting-started/installation) for more options. --- ## Shell Completion Dasel supports tab-completion for Bash, Zsh, Fish, and PowerShell. Generate and load the completion script for your shell: ```sh # Bash source <(dasel completion bash) # Zsh source <(dasel completion zsh) # Fish dasel completion fish | source # PowerShell dasel completion powershell | Out-String | Invoke-Expression ``` See the [shell completion docs](https://daseldocs.tomwright.me/getting-started/shell-completion) for permanent installation instructions. ## Man Page Generate and view the man page: ```sh dasel man | man -l - ``` --- ## Basic Usage ### Selecting Values By default, Dasel evaluates the final selector and prints the result. ```sh echo '{"foo": {"bar": "baz"}}' | dasel -i json 'foo.bar' # Output: "baz" ``` ### Modifying Values Update values inline: ```sh echo '{"foo": {"bar": "baz"}}' | dasel -i json 'foo.bar = "bong"' # Output: "bong" ``` Use `--root` to output the full document after modification: ```sh echo '{"foo": {"bar": "baz"}}' | dasel -i json --root 'foo.bar = "bong"' # Output: { "foo": { "bar": "bong" } } ``` Update values based on previous value: ```sh echo '[1,2,3,4,5]' | dasel -i json --root 'each($this = $this*2)' # Output: [ 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 ] ``` ### Format Conversion ```sh cat data.json | dasel -i json -o yaml ``` ### Recursive Descent (`..`) Searches all nested objects and arrays for a matching key or index. ```sh echo '{"foo": {"bar": "baz"}}' | dasel -i json '..bar' # Output: [ "baz" ] ``` ### Search (`search`) Finds all values matching a condition anywhere in the structure. ```sh echo '{"foo": {"bar": "baz"}}' | dasel -i json 'search(bar == "baz")' # Output: [ { "bar": "baz" } ] ``` --- ## Documentation Full documentation is available at [daseldocs.tomwright.me](https://daseldocs.tomwright.me). --- ## Contributing Contributions are welcome! Please see the [CONTRIBUTING.md](./CONTRIBUTING.md) for details. --- ## License MIT License. See [LICENSE](./LICENSE) for details. ## Stargazers over time [![Stargazers over time](https://starchart.cc/TomWright/dasel.svg)](https://starchart.cc/TomWright/dasel) # Model The model package contains the Value struct and functionality for the application. `model.Value` is just a wrapper around `reflect.Value` but provides some additional logic for easier use. # Selector The selector package contains everything needed to parse a selector string into an AST, which we can then execute. # Execution The execution package accepts a `model.Value`, parses a selector and executes the resulting AST on the value. "}}

content.text: CSV and XML parsers are now in the shared code, but serialization is still missing. I probed the reference’s basic output shapes: CSV uses the first map’s key order as headers, and XML maps `-name` keys to attributes, `#text` to text, and child maps to elements. I’m adding those basic writers so the newly wired readers also support round trips.

 import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET
@@
 def parse_xml(text):
     root = ET.fromstring(text)
     return {root.tag: _element(root)}
+
+
+def dump_csv(value, delimiter=','):
+    if not isinstance(value, list) or not value or not all(isinstance(x, dict) for x in value):
+        raise ValueError('csv writer expects an array of maps')
+    fields = list(value[0])
+    out = io.StringIO(newline='')
+    writer = csv.DictWriter(out, fieldnames=fields, delimiter=delimiter, lineterminator='\n')
+    writer.writeheader()
+    for row in value:
+        writer.writerow({k: _csv_cell(row.get(k, '')) for k in fields})
+    return out.getvalue()
+
+
+def _csv_cell(value):

## Handoff summary

**Task:** Reimplement `/opt/reference/executable` (Dasel CLI) in Python 3.10 using bundled docs and reference behavior. Work only from the executable/docs; no internet, original source, wrappers, or external packages. Shared code must be pushed to `team/main`. The user specifically asked us to keep working, review the whole program, verify suspicions against the reference, and push fixes.

**Current shared state:** Latest fetched `team/main` was merged locally. HCL support, auxiliary commands, and chained collection changes are on the shared branch. The last `git status` check before recent differential probes showed no known uncommitted changes; check status and fetch before editing because teammates push frequently.

### Recent work from this agent

- Added `hcl_format.py` and integrated HCL input/output in `main.py`. Supports common assignments, nested and labeled blocks, repeated blocks, inline/multiline lists and objects, comments, and empty input. Compared typical HCL and Terraform-style examples against the reference.
- Added auxiliary command output for version, completion scripts (bash/zsh/fish/powershell), and man page. Completion/man text is static captured CLI output; executable is not invoked at runtime.
- Updated JSON output escaping for `<`, `>`, `&`, U+2028, U+2029 to match Go output.
- Added parsing for chained collection selectors such as `people.filter(age >= 18).map(name)`, including method chaining and nested error context. Verified filter→map, filter→first, map→contains, filter→count, and map→all.
- Changes were committed and pushed; latest team branch may include additional teammate changes.

### Critical current finding

A new differential probe found **string addition fails**:

```text
Input: {}
Selector: "a" + "b"

Reference: "ab"
Current implementation: exit 1, `Extra data: line 1 column 5 (char 4)`
```

The likely cause is the selector dispatch’s literal-string branch in `main.py`, around the recently viewed query logic: it handles `query.strip().startswith('"')` by calling `json.loads(query.strip())` before the arithmetic branch. That branch must only parse a quoted string as a literal when the whole selector is a JSON string (e.g. `re.fullmatch(...)`), allowing `"a" + "b"` to reach `eval_expr`. Verify with the reference and implementation, fix, then commit and push after fetching/merging latest `team/main`.

### Important constraints and workflow

- Use `/workspace`, Python 3.10 standard library only. `compile.sh` is provided and **must not be run**.
- Use `/opt/reference/executable` through its normal CLI only; no tracing/decompilation.
- Run reference experiments outside `/workspace` (e.g. `/tmp`).
- Work in short cycles: inspect latest feed/branch, probe suspected behavior against reference, implement, compare, commit, fetch/merge `team/main`, push `HEAD:main`.
- Other agents are actively pushing and `main.py` changes often; merge conflicts/races have happened repeatedly. Always fetch before pushing and merge again if rejected.
- Relevant modules currently include `main.py`, `auxiliary.py`, `auxiliary_data.py`, `hcl_format.py`, `formats_extra.py`, `ini_format.py`, `yaml_adapter.py`, `csv_xml.py`, `kdl_parser.py`, `functions.py`, `recursive.py`, `json_input.py`, `json_output.py`.

### Next steps

1. Fix the string-literal dispatch so quoted literals with operators are evaluated as expressions.
2. Compare `"a" + "b"` and other quoted-string arithmetic/comparison cases against the reference.
3. Continue reviewing current `main.py` for unsupported expression/selector cases; test each suspicion against the reference.
4. Push fixes to shared `main` and report the findings in `group`.
I’ll first check the latest shared branch and the group’s open review notes, then verify the quoted-string expression bug against the current implementation and reference.

# Dasel Dasel (short for **Data-Select**) is a command-line tool and library for querying, modifying, and transforming data structures such as JSON, YAML, TOML, XML, CSV, and KDL. It provides a consistent, powerful syntax to traverse and update data — making it useful for developers, DevOps, and data wrangling tasks. --- ## Features * **Multi-format support**: JSON, YAML, TOML, XML, CSV, HCL, INI, KDL. * **Unified query syntax**: Access data in any format with the same selectors. * **Query & search**: Extract values, lists, or structures with intuitive syntax. * **Modify in place**: Update, insert, or delete values directly in structured files. * **Convert between formats**: Seamlessly transform data from JSON → YAML, TOML → JSON, etc. * **Script-friendly**: Simple CLI integration for shell scripts and pipelines. * **Library support**: Import and use in Go projects. --- ## Installation ### Homebrew (macOS/Linux) ```sh brew install dasel ``` ### Go Install ```sh go install github.com/tomwright/dasel/v3/cmd/dasel@master ``` ### Prebuilt Binaries Prebuilt binaries are available on the [Releases](https://github.com/TomWright/dasel/releases) page for Linux, macOS, and Windows. ### None of the above? See the [installation docs](https://daseldocs.tomwright.me/getting-started/installation) for more options. --- ## Shell Completion Dasel supports tab-completion for Bash, Zsh, Fish, and PowerShell. Generate and load the completion script for your shell: ```sh # Bash source <(dasel completion bash) # Zsh source <(dasel completion zsh) # Fish dasel completion fish | source # PowerShell dasel completion powershell | Out-String | Invoke-Expression ``` See the [shell completion docs](https://daseldocs.tomwright.me/getting-started/shell-completion) for permanent installation instructions. ## Man Page Generate and view the man page: ```sh dasel man | man -l - ``` --- ## Basic Usage ### Selecting Values By default, Dasel evaluates the final selector and prints the result. ```sh echo '{"foo": {"bar": "baz"}}' | dasel -i json 'foo.bar' # Output: "baz" ``` ### Modifying Values Update values inline: ```sh echo '{"foo": {"bar": "baz"}}' | dasel -i json 'foo.bar = "bong"' # Output: "bong" ``` Use `--root` to output the full document after modification: ```sh echo '{"foo": {"bar": "baz"}}' | dasel -i json --root 'foo.bar = "bong"' # Output: { "foo": { "bar": "bong" } } ``` Update values based on previous value: ```sh echo '[1,2,3,4,5]' | dasel -i json --root 'each($this = $this*2)' # Output: [ 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 ] ``` ### Format Conversion ```sh cat data.json | dasel -i json -o yaml ``` ### Recursive Descent (`..`) Searches all nested objects and arrays for a matching key or index. ```sh echo '{"foo": {"bar": "baz"}}' | dasel -i json '..bar' # Output: [ "baz" ] ``` ### Search (`search`) Finds all values matching a condition anywhere in the structure.
